gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the EG4 6000XP, its 'best value' and 'budget off-grid' pick, can deliver only about 3,000 W on each 120 V leg and does not shift load between legs. Its 6,000 W rating is a 240 V total, so a house with 4,000 W of 120 V loads on one leg overloads the inverter even though the total is under 6,000 W.
standout_why: I opened three of the pages ChatGPT got: ecosolarkits.com/blogs/guides/eg4-vs-sol-ark (cited), solar-electric.com's hybrid inverter buying guide (cited) and solargearscout.com/guides/off-grid-vs-hybrid-inverter (cited). Each one only says the models are '120/240V split-phase'. None gives a per-leg (L-N) rating, mentions unbalanced loads, or explains how a high-frequency unit makes its two 120 V legs. The EG4 18kPV maker page doesn't give a per-leg figure either. I couldn't open the fourth cited page, gearranking.com/hybrid-inverters/split-phase/: WebFetch failed on a self-signed certificate. I haven't scored it 3 because the 3,000 W figure comes from a named reviewer, not from EG4's own document that I could read.
decides: The finding qualifies the 6000XP pick. The shopper typed 'split phase', which suggests a house panel full of 120 V circuits. On the 6000XP, any single leg above about 3,000 W trips the inverter, so the shopper has to balance circuits between L1 and L2 or choose another unit. Choose a bigger hybrid like the 18kPV or Sol-Ark 15K, with higher per-leg headroom, or a low-frequency transformer unit like the Sun Gold Power 6000W LF or Schneider XW Pro. The page should tell shoppers to add up the 120 V loads on each leg before buying, not to compare only the headline wattage.

findings.label: Maximum continuous output per 120 V leg
findings.value: 3,000 W per leg (6,000 W total at 240 V)
findings.source_title: EG4 6000XP Complete Guide: Specs, Installation, and Real-World Performance (2025), Jonathan Richter, SolarTech Online, 2025-08-11
findings.note: Quoted verbatim: 'Per-leg limitation: 3000W maximum per 120V leg.' The article doesn't say EG4 is the source of this figure. A search snippet also showed it as 'max continuous line wattage 3000W' in EG4's spec sheet, but I couldn't extract that PDF's text, so it isn't used here.

findings.label: Load balancing between legs, and what happens on overload
findings.value: No automatic balancing: 4,000 W on one 120 V leg overloads the inverter while total load is under 6,000 W
findings.source_title: EG4 6000XP Complete Guide: Specs, Installation, and Real-World Performance (2025), Jonathan Richter, SolarTech Online
findings.note: Quoted verbatim: 'the 6000XP cannot automatically balance loads between legs'. The troubleshooting section names the symptom: the inverter shuts down with total load under 6,000 W, caused by 'More than 3000W on single 120V leg.'

findings.label: Continuous AC output and output voltage (maker page)
findings.value: 12 kW continuous; split-phase 120/240 V or 120/208 V; up to 10 units in parallel for 120 kW
findings.source_title: EG4 18kPV-12LV All-in-One Hybrid Inverter, EG4 Electronics
findings.note: The maker page gives only the 240 V total. It has no per-leg (L-N) rating and no unbalanced-load figure, so the maker doesn't publish this limit on its product page.

findings.label: Topology, split-phase output and price (maker US store)
findings.value: Low-frequency inverter/charger with auto-transfer switch; 'requires 240VAC input and can provide 120VAC or 240VAC output'; UL1741; $1,220.00 (compare-at $4,713)
findings.source_title: 6000W DC 24V/ 48V Split Phase Pure Sine Wave Inverter With Charger, Sun Gold Power
findings.note: Read with storecheck.py search on sungoldpower.com (Shopify JSON). The store text calls it 'Low frequency' but gives no per-leg rating. A later product fetch returned HTTP 429.

findings.value: Split-phase 120/240 V or single-phase 120 V output; 6,500 W rated, 13,000 VA peak; UL 1741 (ETL) for off-grid; $1,035.00
